COMPUTER SOFTWARE EMPLOYEE OVERTIME EXEMPTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Corp.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's computer software employee overtime exemption, codified at Labor Code § 515.5, in connection with the position of Senior Software Engineer held or to be held by Jane Doe at Acme Corp.

Labor Code § 515.5 is a separate and independent statutory exemption from the general executive, administrative, and professional exemptions addressed elsewhere in this corpus's Exempt / Non-Exempt Classification Notice document. Those general exemptions are established by the Industrial Welfare Commission under Labor Code § 515(a) and depend on a duties test plus a salary set as a multiple of the state minimum wage. Section 515.5 instead sets its own specific duties criteria and its own specific, dollar-denominated rate-of-pay floor, adjusted annually by the Department of Industrial Relations, that is not tied to the minimum wage. A position can potentially qualify for the Section 515.5 exemption without qualifying for the general exemptions, and vice versa — meeting one test does not by itself show that the other is met.

This information sheet does not itself determine that Jane Doe's position at Acme Corp. does or does not qualify for the Section 515.5 exemption, does not apply this test to any specific facts, does not investigate or make any finding about any specific position, and does not file anything with any agency or court.

CALIFORNIA'S OVERTIME DEFAULT AND HOW THE COMPUTER SOFTWARE EXEMPTION DIFFERS FROM THE GENERAL EXEMPTIONS
California law generally requires overtime compensation for work beyond eight hours in a workday or 40 hours in a workweek, and for the first eight hours worked on a seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek, at not less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay under Labor Code § 510. Labor Code § 515.5(a) provides that, except as stated in its own subdivision (b), an employee in the computer software field is exempt from this Section 510 overtime requirement if the criteria described below are all met.

This is a structurally different path to exemption than the one Labor Code § 515(a) provides for executive, administrative, and professional employees. Section 515(a) authorizes the Industrial Welfare Commission to establish those exemptions where the employee is primarily engaged in duties meeting an IWC-adopted duties test and earns a monthly salary equivalent to at least two times the state minimum wage. Section 515.5, by contrast, is a self-contained statutory exemption: its duties criteria are written into the statute itself rather than adopted by IWC regulation, and its rate-of-pay requirement is a specific dollar figure adjusted annually by the Department of Industrial Relations based on a consumer price index, independent of the state minimum wage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=510.)
  "(a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), an employee in the computer software field shall be exempt from the requirement that an overtime rate of compensation be paid pursuant to Section 510 if all of the following apply:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.5.)
  "(a) The Industrial Welfare Commission may establish exemptions from the requirement that an overtime rate of compensation be paid pursuant to Sections 510 and 511 for executive, administrative, and professional employees, if the employee is primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.)
  Known gap: Labor Code §§ 515.5(a) and 515(a) are independent statutory sections (515.5 is not a subdivision of 515); § 510 is likewise an independent section that both 515 and 515.5 reference as the overtime requirement they provide exemptions from. This clause does not address Labor Code § 511 (alternative workweek schedules), § 514 (exemptions under a qualifying collective bargaining agreement), the outside salesperson exemption, or the separate federal FLSA computer employee exemption (29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(17)) — none of those are covered by this document. It also does not address the remainder of § 515 (subdivisions (b) through (f), covering matters such as the treatment of nonexempt salaried employees' regular rate and special rules for registered nurses), which are not relevant to the Section 515.5 computer software exemption described here.

THE COMPUTER SOFTWARE EMPLOYEE DUTIES AND SKILL TEST
Labor Code § 515.5(a) lists four conditions that must all apply for the exemption to be available; the first three describe the nature of the work and the employee's skill level. The employee must be primarily engaged in work that is intellectual or creative and that requires the exercise of discretion and independent judgment. The employee must also be primarily engaged in duties consisting of one or more of: applying systems analysis techniques and procedures (including consulting with users) to determine hardware, software, or system functional specifications; the design, development, documentation, analysis, creation, testing, or modification of computer systems or programs, including prototypes, based on and related to user or system design specifications; or the documentation, testing, creation, or modification of computer programs related to the design of software or hardware for computer operating systems. Finally, the employee must be highly skilled and proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, or software engineering. The statute itself states that a job title is not determinative of whether this exemption applies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(1) The employee is primarily engaged in work that is intellectual or creative and that requires the exercise of discretion and independent judgment. (2) The employee is primarily engaged in duties that consist of one or more of the following: (A) The application of systems analysis techniques and procedures, including consulting with users, to determine hardware, software, or system functional specifications. (B) The design, development, documentation, analysis, creation, testing, or modification of computer systems or programs, including prototypes, based on and related to user or system design specifications. (C) The documentation, testing, creation, or modification of computer programs related to the design of software or hardware for computer operating systems. (3) The employee is highly skilled and is proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, or software engineering. A job title shall not be determinative of the applicability of this exemption."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(a)(1)-(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.5.)
  Known gap: This clause covers Labor Code § 515.5(a)(1) through (a)(3) — three of the four paragraphs within subdivision (a) of the same statutory section as the rate-of-pay requirement covered in a separate clause of this document (§ 515.5(a)(4)). All four paragraphs of subdivision (a) must be satisfied together for the exemption to apply; meeting the duties and skill criteria in (1) through (3) without also meeting the rate-of-pay requirement in (4) does not qualify a position for this exemption, and vice versa. This clause also does not cover subdivision (b)'s exclusions, which are addressed in a separate clause, and it does not determine whether any specific employee's actual duties meet this test.

THE MINIMUM RATE-OF-PAY REQUIREMENT AND ITS STATUTORY ADJUSTMENT MECHANISM
As the fourth condition of the Labor Code § 515.5(a) test, the employee's hourly rate of pay must not be less than a specific statutory dollar figure, or, if the employee is paid on a salaried basis, the employee must earn an annual salary of not less than a specific statutory figure for full-time employment, paid at least once a month in a monthly amount of not less than a further specific statutory figure. The statute's own codified text — last amended in 2012 — prints these figures as $36.00 per hour, $75,000 per year, and $6,250 per month. But the statute does not leave those figures fixed: by its own terms, the Department of Industrial Relations is directed to adjust both the hourly rate and the salary levels every October 1, effective the following January 1, by the percentage increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Because that adjustment is made administratively by the department rather than by amending the statute's printed text, the dollar figures appearing in the codified version of Section 515.5 are the figures as last set by the Legislature (2012) and do not, by themselves, reflect the current operative amount for any given year.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(4) The employee’s hourly rate of pay is not less than thirty-six dollars ($36.00) or, if the employee is paid on a salaried basis, the employee earns an annual salary of not less than seventy-five thousand dollars ($75,000) for full-time employment, which is paid at least once a month and in a monthly amount of not less than six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($6,250). The department shall adjust both the hourly pay rate and the salary level described in this paragraph on October 1 of each year to be effective on January 1 of the following year by an amount equal to the percentage increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.5.)
  Known gap: This clause covers Labor Code § 515.5(a)(4) only — the fourth paragraph of the same subdivision (a) whose first three paragraphs (the duties and skill test) are covered in a separate clause of this document. The $36.00/hour, $75,000/year, and $6,250/month figures quoted here are the statute's own printed baseline as of its last legislative amendment (2012); they are not represented as the current operative figures for any particular year. The actual dollar figure the Department of Industrial Relations has most recently published under this adjustment mechanism, as independently verified from the department's own publication, is stated in a separate clause of this document.

THE DEPARTMENT OF INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS' MOST RECENTLY PUBLISHED ADJUSTED RATE
The Department of Industrial Relations publishes the dollar figures that result from the annual Labor Code § 515.5(a)(4) adjustment described above. As of the date this clause was verified, the department's own published notice states that, in accordance with Section 515.5(a)(4), it adjusted the computer software employee's minimum hourly rate of pay exemption from $56.97 to $58.85, the minimum monthly salary exemption from $9,888.13 to $10,214.44, and the minimum annual salary exemption from $118,657.43 to $122,573.13, effective January 1, 2026, reflecting a 3.3% increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers measured from August 2024 to August 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In accordance with Labor Code Section 515.5(a)(4), the department has adjusted the computer software employee’s minimum hourly rate of pay exemption from $56.97 to $58.85, the minimum monthly salary exemption from $9,888.13 to $10,214.44, and the minimum annual salary exemption from $118,657.43 to $122,573.13 effective January 1, 2026, reflecting the 3.3% increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers."
  — California Department of Industrial Relations, Overtime Exemption for Computer Software Employees (Office of the Director – Research, effective January 1, 2026), California Department of Industrial Relations (https://www.dir.ca.gov/oprl/ComputerSoftware.htm)
  Known gap: This clause reports the figures published by the Department of Industrial Relations as of the checkedDate above, drawn directly from the department's own webpage rather than from the codified statutory text (which prints only the 2012 baseline figures, covered in a separate clause of this document). The department's notice states these figures took effect January 1, 2026 and were calculated from the department's own August 2024-to-August 2025 index comparison. By the statute's own adjustment mechanism, the department recalculates and republishes new figures each October for the following January 1 — meaning a later adjustment (for January 1, 2027 and beyond) will supersede the figures quoted here, and this document's text does not update itself as new figures are published. This clause does not address the parallel computer software employee exemption language found in the applicable IWC wage order, which restates a version of this same dollar threshold.

STATUTORY EXCLUSIONS FROM THE EXEMPTION
Labor Code § 515.5(b) states that the exemption described in subdivision (a) does not apply to an employee if any of six listed circumstances apply. Those circumstances are: the employee is a trainee or entry-level employee still learning to become proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, and software engineering; the employee is in a computer-related occupation but has not attained the level of skill and expertise necessary to work independently and without close supervision; the employee is engaged in the operation of computers or in the manufacture, repair, or maintenance of computer hardware and related equipment; the employee is an engineer, drafter, machinist, or other professional whose work is highly dependent upon or facilitated by computers and computer software (including someone skilled in computer-aided design software such as CAD/CAM) but who is not engaged in computer systems analysis, programming, or another similarly skilled computer-related occupation; the employee is a writer of material such as box labels, product descriptions, documentation, promotional material, or setup and installation instructions, whether for print or onscreen media, or who provides content intended to be read by customers, subscribers, or visitors to computer-related media such as the web or CD-ROMs; or the employee is engaged in the subdivision (a) duties for the purpose of creating imagery for effects used in the motion picture, television, or theatrical industry.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) The exemption provided in subdivision (a) does not apply to an employee if any of the following apply: (1) The employee is a trainee or employee in an entry-level position who is learning to become proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, and software engineering. (2) The employee is in a computer-related occupation but has not attained the level of skill and expertise necessary to work independently and without close supervision. (3) The employee is engaged in the operation of computers or in the manufacture, repair, or maintenance of computer hardware and related equipment. (4) The employee is an engineer, drafter, machinist, or other professional whose work is highly dependent upon or facilitated by the use of computers and computer software programs and who is skilled in computer-aided design software, including CAD/CAM, but who is not engaged in computer systems analysis, programming, or any other similarly skilled computer-related occupation. (5) The employee is a writer engaged in writing material, including box labels, product descriptions, documentation, promotional material, setup and installation instructions, and other similar written information, either for print or for onscreen media or who writes or provides content material intended to be read by customers, subscribers, or visitors to computer-related media such as the World Wide Web or CD-ROMs. (6) The employee is engaged in any of the activities set forth in subdivision (a) for the purpose of creating imagery for effects used in the motion picture, television, or theatrical industry."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=515.5.)
  Known gap: This clause covers Labor Code § 515.5(b), an independent subdivision of the same statutory section as subdivision (a) covered in this document's other authority clauses. The statute does not itself define terms such as 'trainee,' 'entry-level position,' or 'close supervision' used within this list, and this clause does not supply definitions for those terms or determine whether any specific employee's circumstances fall within any of the six listed exclusions.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — COMPUTER SOFTWARE EMPLOYEE EXEMPTION INFORMATION SHEET
